To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
microtubules regulate the extracellular release of poliovirus by controlling the mobility of autophagosome-derived vesicles.
poliovirus induces the formation of autophagosome like vesicles that are tethered by microtubules to the plasma membrane.
poliovirus induces the formation of double membrane vesicles that are tethered to microtubules.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms by which poliovirus and other viruses exit the infected cell and spread to neighboring cells.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate the release of infectious poliovirus from the cytoplasm of infected cells.
the role of microtubules in extracellular release of poliovirus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

microtubule disruption increases the release of poliovirus from infected cells by enhancing the fusion of autophagosome-derived double-membraned cytosolic vesicles with the plasma membrane, which is consistent to the hypothesis that small amount of cytosol could be released via membrane fusion with the plasma.
the microtubule network is involved in the release of poliovirus, and that the release of virus and cellular contents is dependent on the interaction of viral capsid proteins with the cytoskeleton.

poliovirus infection induces autophagosome formation that is tethered to the microtubular system, and this tethered autophagosome is the site of extracellular delivery of poliovirus and cytoplasmic content.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the microtubule-dependent tethering of double membrane vesicles is a novel mechanism for the release of cytosolic contents, including infectious agents, from infected cells.
poliovirus subverts the host cytoskeletal network to promote its own release.

we have shown that the poliovirus-induced double-membraned cytoplasmic vesicles are immobile in infected cells, that they become motile upon nocodazole or BFA treatment, and that this mobility correlates with an increase in the amount of extracellular virus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
poliovirus induces autophagy-like structures that are tethered by microtubules and that the release of these autophagosomes-like structures is a key step in poliovirus release.

poliovirus can induce the formation of autophagosomes-like vesicles and that these vesicles can be released to the extracellular space via a microtubule-dependent tethering mechanism that is likely to be conserved in many viruses.
poliovirus can use the autophagic pathway to exit cells without causing cell lysis.
